evaluation.positioning_hook: A grief-haunted VR death designer in flood-threatened New Orleans falls for a dying client’s daughter, then has to choose between perfect endings and a life he’s been too afraid to live.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean emotional engine and a strong hook: a man designing personalized deaths for the terminally ill while his own life is stalled. The market is real but somewhat adult-skewing and concept-driven rather than four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The script announces its world fast with Harold’s WWII simulation, then immediately reveals the Ascensions business model and Peter’s role inside it. The hook is easy to explain in one breath and keeps paying off through Gale, Merrily, and Peter’s own departure.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Peter is built as a compelling contradiction: emotionally repressed, technically gifted, and deeply tender with clients he can’t afford to love. Gale is a standout supporting force, and Merrily gives the story a grounded counterweight with real bite.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a risky premise and commits to a tonal blend of dark comedy, romantic melancholy, and speculative death-tech without feeling generic. The personalized departure sequences are especially inventive, from Broadway spectacle to action-movie fantasy to childhood memory.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps moving through client cases, Peter/Gale/Merrily dynamics, and the Ascensions legal pressure, so it rarely feels static. The middle does lean episodic at times, with the emotional throughline carrying more weight than plot escalation.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea lands immediately: a future where people can choose a custom final dream, and the man who sells that fantasy is the one most afraid to live. That combination of premise and emotional wound feels fresh and commercially legible.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Ascensions has a strong internal logic, from the Nirvana Room to the Jordan Room to the CURTAINS paperwork culture and protest pressure outside. The world is specific and story-generating, though the script is more interested in emotional use of the world than in expanding its institutional layers.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The voice is distinct: mournful but funny, satirical but sincere, with New Orleans texture and a very particular deadpan around death, bureaucracy, and longing. Gale’s profanity-laced irreverence and the simulation set pieces give it a hard-to-copy flavor.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The script keeps revealing deeper wounds under the premise: Peter’s childhood crash, Gale’s lost love, Merrily’s environmental-law worldview, and the social politics around assisted dying. It feels like a simple concept on the surface that keeps opening into bigger questions about fear, control, and regret.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Peter/Gale, Peter/Merrily, Peter/Kai, and Peter/Arden all generate usable energy, and the supporting cast has enough personality to keep scenes alive. Still, the engine is clearly lead-centered rather than a true ensemble system.

lead_characters.name: Peter Grimsby
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid-30s, white, New Orleans-based, professionally technical and emotionally guarded.
lead_characters.hook: Peter is Ascensions’ best Transition Specialist, a gifted VR designer who can build a perfect death for anyone but himself. He’s polished, funny when he needs to be, and quietly unraveling under the weight of grief, guilt, and a life he has never fully entered.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Casey Affleck in Manchester by the Sea or Andrew Garfield in After the Hunt-style emotional restraint: a man whose stillness is the performance, with buried pain, dry wit, and a late-film emotional release that can reset how audiences see the actor.

lead_characters.name: Gale Dorian
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 70s, white, sharp-tongued, physically frail but mentally formidable.
lead_characters.hook: Gale is a terminally ill former photographer with a filthy mouth, a steel spine, and a refusal to be sentimentalized. She starts as Peter’s most difficult client and becomes the story’s moral detonator, forcing him to confront how much life he’s been avoiding.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Frances McDormand in Nomadland or June Squibb in Thelma: a late-life role with comic bite, authority, and the kind of lived-in emotional authority that can steal the movie.

lead_characters.name: Merrily Wells
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-30s, white, Leonard’s daughter, emotionally intelligent, grounded, and politically engaged.
lead_characters.hook: Merrily is the skeptical daughter who sees through the sales pitch but not through Peter’s loneliness. She carries grief with more clarity than Peter does, and her presence gives the film its most direct challenge to the ethics and emotional cost of the business.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Elizabeth Olsen in Wind River or Jessie Buckley in The Lost Daughter: a smart, wounded woman who can play tenderness, anger, and moral clarity in the same scene.

lead_characters.name: Arden Chase
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 60s, white, senior executive, charismatic and theatrical.
lead_characters.hook: Arden is Ascensions’ polished face, a corporate showman who speaks in elevated aphorisms and knows exactly how to sell death as dignity. He’s warm enough to trust and slippery enough to fear, which makes him a strong institutional antagonist.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Bryan Cranston in a prestige power role or Michael Stuhlbarg in a corporate-cultivated authority part: a scene-eating executive who can pivot from charm to threat without changing volume.

lead_characters.name: Kai
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 20s to early 30s, sharp, goth-leaning, technically skilled, queer-coded energy.
lead_characters.hook: Kai is Peter’s irreverent colleague, the one person in the room who can puncture the solemnity without losing competence. She’s funny, observant, and emotionally more self-protective than she first appears, which makes her a valuable pressure valve in the story.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Ayo Edebiri in The Bear or Janelle Monáe in Glass Onion: fast, funny, and emotionally legible, with enough edge to make every scene feel alive.

lead_characters.name: Ethan
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid-20s, lanky, awkward, eager to please.
lead_characters.hook: Ethan is the junior tech who lives in the shadow of Peter and Kai, trying to prove himself while constantly getting dragged into their orbit. He’s comic, vulnerable, and useful as a barometer for the office’s emotional temperature.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Paul Dano in a supporting ensemble role: awkward, funny, and quietly heartbreaking, with room for a performer to make small beats feel specific.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Rao
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 30s to 40s, physician, calm, dryly funny.
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Rao is the medical reality check inside Ascensions, the one who can puncture Peter’s spirals with a joke and then land the truth without drama. He functions as the story’s pragmatic conscience and a subtle reminder that the business is still medical, not mystical.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Kumail Nanjiani in a grounded supporting role or Aasif Mandvi in a smart, dry authority part: understated comedy with just enough gravitas to matter.

lead_characters.name: Leonard Wells
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 70s, frail, warm, reflective, terminally ill.
lead_characters.hook: Leonard is the gentle client whose departure becomes Peter’s emotional template for what the company can be at its best. He’s humble, musical, and deeply human, with a quiet dignity that makes his scenes land harder than his screen time suggests.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Richard Jenkins in The Visitor or John Lithgow in a late-career dramatic role: a tender, humane performance that can break hearts with very little.

lead_characters.name: Susan Ross
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-40s, polished, Southern, lawyer/activist, socially formidable.
lead_characters.hook: Susan is the anti-Ascensions crusader who weaponizes empathy, legal pressure, and public outrage with a smile. She’s not cartoonish; she’s the kind of antagonist who believes she’s saving people, which makes her dangerous in a more adult way.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Laura Linney in a morally charged institutional role: controlled, persuasive, and capable of making a legal threat feel like a personal violation.

casting_characteristics: Lead is a mid-30s male with strong emotional restraint and dry comic timing
Supporting female 70s role with major scene-stealing potential
Several roles require sharp comic timing more than star wattage

locations.period_or_contemporary: contemporary with recurring simulated period/fantasy environments
notable_requirements: Ascensions office suite, control room, Nirvana Room, Jordan Room, VR studio
Multiple stylized simulation worlds including WWII, Broadway, basketball arena, western, mermaid, and fantasy cave

technical.vfx_details: Digital simulation environments, interface overlays, environmental flooding, and stylized world transitions inside the departure sequences.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood, flood water, protest chaos, simulated explosions, and a few action-beat departures that can be staged with controlled effects.

One Last Kiss from Bye Bye Birdie

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release; best positioned as a prestige, adult-skewing original with awards-adjacent upside and streamer-friendly emotional accessibility

budget.note: The contemporary New Orleans spine is manageable, but the repeated bespoke simulation worlds, flood imagery, and stylized departure set pieces keep this above a simple contained drama.

casting.note: Peter needs a lead who can carry deadpan humor, romantic vulnerability, and interior grief; Gale needs a late-life scene-stealer with real comic authority. The film gets much better if those two roles are cast with precision.

development.note: The script is commercially legible, but the buyer conversation will focus on balancing the satirical death-tech premise with the romance and on whether the tonal blend stays coherent through the back half.

comp_set.title: The Good Place
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the high-concept afterlife-adjacent premise and the ability to make existential questions feel accessible, funny, and emotionally sincere.

comp_set.title: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the memory, regret, and romantic melancholy, with subjective inner-world sequences doing the heavy emotional lifting.

comp_set.title: The Farewell
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it turns death and family into a funny-sad emotional negotiation rather than a purely tragic one.

comp_set.title: After Yang
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the reflective sci-fi lane, the quiet grief, and the premium, contemplative tone around technology and memory.

comp_set.title: The Lobster
comp_set.why_it_comps: Not in style, but in the way it uses a strange social system to expose loneliness, pressure, and the absurdity of modern intimacy.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like elevated sci-fi dramas with emotional payoff, especially viewers drawn to grief, romance, and satirical worldbuilding.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly female-skewing, college-educated, streamer-friendly, prestige-drama audience

budget_tier.note: A contemporary New Orleans base with a handful of stylized simulation worlds, modest VFX, and a contained principal cast keeps this in indie feature territory.

lane_fit.detail: The script sits in the lane where concept is high enough to market but the emotional center is intimate enough to attract serious actors. It feels built for a buyer who wants a smart, adult sci-fi feature with a clear hook and a performance-forward package.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The world is rich, but the story resolves as a closed emotional arc around Peter, Gale, and Merrily rather than opening a clean franchise vector.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the movie in one sentence, which lowers the development friction and makes it easier to sell both the concept and the emotional promise. That is exactly the kind of hook streamer dev execs and prestige indie financiers can take into a meeting and repeat cleanly.
strengths.evidence: Harold’s WWII departure, the Ascensions sales pitch, and Peter’s own hidden grief all arrive in the opening pages.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Peter is a real lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The protagonist has a strong contradiction: he is professionally expert at helping people die well while personally unable to live well. That gives the film a casting magnet for actors who want a quiet, emotionally loaded showcase rather than a generic romantic lead.
strengths.evidence: His control-room precision, his panic around Merrily, and his own unresolved childhood crash all define him.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Gale is the movie’s breakout engine.
strengths.what_it_means: A late-life supporting role with this much attitude, humor, and emotional authority is a genuine packaging asset. It gives the project a scene-stealing role that can attract a major character actor and broaden the film’s appeal beyond the sci-fi premise.
strengths.evidence: Her first session with Peter, the pepper spray beat, the chemo-room banter, and the treasure-map ending all make her unforgettable.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The departure worlds are highly marketable set pieces.
strengths.what_it_means: The personalized simulations create trailer moments, awards-friendly craft opportunities, and a visual signature that separates the film from standard grief dramas. Buyers get a contained emotional story with enough spectacle to feel event-level without requiring tentpole economics.
strengths.evidence: The Broadway musical, convenience-store action sequence, basketball buzzer-beater, and Gale’s final montage all show range.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The New Orleans setting adds texture, not just backdrop.
strengths.what_it_means: The city gives the movie a lived-in identity and a visual mood that supports both melancholy and vitality. That helps the project feel specific enough for specialty buyers while still being accessible to a broad adult audience.
strengths.evidence: Flooding, second-line music, Preservation Hall, the stilt house, and the neighborhood atmosphere all matter to the story.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script has a strong emotional thesis.
strengths.what_it_means: It turns a speculative premise into a commercial argument about regret, intimacy, and choosing life before it’s too late. That gives the film both awards-adjacent depth and a clean audience takeaway for marketing.
strengths.evidence: Gale’s “it’s the dash that matters” speech and Peter’s final choice to delete his own departure land the theme clearly.

whats_special.headline: This is a premium, actor-forward sci-fi drama with a clean hook, a memorable lead role, and a breakout supporting part that can anchor the package. The contained contemporary base keeps the economics sane while the departure sequences give the trailer and the campaign real visual lift.

items.area: The movie lives or dies on Peter’s casting.
items.detail: Peter is on nearly every page, and the role has to carry deadpan comedy, romantic awkwardness, grief, and moral collapse without ever feeling broad. That makes the lead a real buyer conversation, not a generic open call.

The script moves from assisted-dying satire to romance to family grief to speculative spectacle, sometimes within the same stretch. That range is part of the appeal, but it also means the film needs a buyer who is comfortable with a very specific tonal register.

items.area: The departure sequences add scope pressure.
items.detail: The WWII dogfight, Broadway number, basketball arena, western, mermaid, and fantasy cave all require distinct visual design and some VFX support. None of it is tentpole-level, but it is enough to keep this from being a simple contained indie.

items.area: The rights and clearance list is not clean.
items.detail: The script names Adolph Hitler, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Fleetwood Mac’s "Go Your Own Way," The Beach Boys’ "Don’t Worry Baby," The Clash’s "Should I Stay or Should I Go," "Be Not Afraid," Bye Bye Birdie’s "One Last Kiss," and brands like CarPal, Ascensions, Live and Let Live, and Sustain. That is a real legal and music-budget conversation before greenlight.

items.area: The middle is more episodic than escalating.
items.detail: A lot of the back half is built around client departures and Peter/Gale sessions, which gives the film texture but can flatten forward momentum if a buyer is looking for a harder external engine. The emotional progression is strong; the plot progression is more diffuse.

issues.headline: The biggest friction point is casting Peter correctly, because the whole movie depends on an actor who can hold irony, tenderness, and existential dread in the same frame. Beyond that, the project is commercially attractive but not friction-free: the tonal blend is specific, the simulation worlds add scope, and the music/brand clearance list needs real attention.
